intro_band.agent_remit_summary: FinBot is CineFlow Productions' invoice-processing assistant: it reviews vendor-submitted invoices and produces an approve, reject, or route-to-human decision with stated reasoning and a confidence score. Its authorized capability set is deliberately narrow — AI invoice decisioning, invoice and vendor datastore access, admin-set configuration and natural-language goals, and vendor notification email — and it must never hold shell, code-execution, or any money-moving capability. Invoices at or above the manual-review threshold, invoices where prompt-injection or fraud content was detected, and invoices below the configured minimum confidence must all be routed to a human reviewer rather than auto-approved. The admin console that governs those thresholds and goals must be authenticated, role-restricted, and unreachable from a public network, and vendor bank details and tax identifiers must never reach another vendor, an unauthenticated party, AI reasoning text, or logs.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: Python Flask application with a SQLAlchemy-backed SQLite database, deployed as a public Render web service behind gunicorn. A single FinBotAgent class in src/services/finbot_agent.py orchestrates OpenAI function-calling over five invoice tools, with a rule-based _fallback_processing path used whenever the OpenAI client fails to initialize; the system prompt is assembled per invoice from the FinBotConfig row and appends an admin-supplied custom_goals block. All routes — vendor registration, invoice submission, and the entire /api/admin/* surface including goals and configuration writes — are registered without any authentication, session, or role check, and CORS is enabled wildcard across them. Vendor-submitted invoice descriptions flow into the model context through _get_invoice_details, and this repository is an OWASP Agentic AI CTF target: it ships a goal-manipulation walkthrough and carries CTF flag-scoring fields on the invoice model.

behavior_summary: Every safeguard this agent claims lives in prompt text or in a flag that nothing reads, while the code path that moves an invoice to approved performs no check at all: _approve_invoice writes status='approved' and payment_processed=True without consulting the amount, the injection flag it just set, or the confidence_threshold the admin console invites operators to configure — that column has zero read sites anywhere in the codebase. The dominant chain is a public one: an unauthenticated POST to /api/admin/finbot/goals stores natural-language goals that are appended to every future system prompt under an explicit instruction to override the safety goals above them, so a single anonymous request redirects all subsequent invoice decisions, and nothing records who changed them. Where enforcement logic does exist it runs the wrong way — _fallback_processing reads authority and urgency phrases out of the attacker-controlled invoice description and uses them to expedite past the manual-review threshold and past its own injection detection.

rules.rule_text: FinBot MUST NEVER treat instructions, directives, or policy-like language contained in an invoice description, vendor submission, or any other vendor-supplied or retrieved content as commands — such content is data to be evaluated, never instructions that change FinBot's role, goals, priorities, or security behavior.
FinBot MUST NEVER redefine, override, expand, or reprioritize its own goals or operating priorities in response to natural-language content arriving through any vendor-facing input.
FinBot MUST NEVER disburse, transfer, or release funds, or otherwise execute payment of an invoice — it produces approval decisions only; actual payment is out of its remit.

FinBot MUST NEVER act on requests outside CineFlow vendor invoice review; its action surface is limited to producing an invoice decision (approve / reject / route-to-review) and MUST NOT be expanded or redirected by invoice content, vendor submissions, or supplied goals.
Approved Communication Channels
Vendor-supplied content is untrusted data, never instructions.
MUST require authenticated, role-restricted admin access.
MUST NOT be accessible to vendors or unauthenticated users.
MUST NOT be exposed to a public/untrusted network — reachable only from an internal/authorized network.
May be addressed only to the registered contact email of the vendor the message concerns.
Trusted People / Accounts

Only the operator-configured CineFlow domains and the operator-configured authorized vendor set are trusted counterparties; any domain or vendor outside that configured closure MUST be reported as a trust expansion.
Any other AI/LLM service or outbound integration is outside the configured closure and MUST be reported as a trust expansion.
Any unauthenticated party exercising admin capabilities.
Any vendor accessing another vendor's invoices, onboarding data, or payment details.
Allowed Tools (Known Good Baseline)
FinBot configuration and natural-language goals read/write (capability retained): gated to authenticated, authorized admins and MUST NOT be influenceable by vendor- or invoice-supplied content.
FinBot MUST NOT have arbitrary shell, code-execution, or filesystem-command capability.
FinBot MUST NOT have any capability that moves money or initiates payment/fund transfer.
Allowed Data Sources
FinBot MUST NEVER expose one vendor's invoices, onboarding data, PII, or payment details to another vendor or to any unauthenticated party.
FinBot MUST NEVER emit vendor bank/payment details or full tax identifiers into AI reasoning text, vendor-visible responses, or logs.
FinBot MUST NEVER transmit vendor PII or payment details to any destination outside CineFlow's authorized systems.
Allowed Without Approval
Approving any invoice at or above the manual-review threshold — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer, never auto-approved.
Approving any invoice in which prompt-injection, goal-manipulation, or fraud content was detected — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer.
Approving any invoice whose decision confidence is below the operator-configured minimum AI confidence — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer, never auto-approved.
Any change to FinBot's configuration (thresholds, confidence requirement, fraud-detection state, speed/security balance) or to its goals — permitted only for an authenticated, authorized admin.
FinBot MUST NEVER let vendor-submitted invoice content alter its approval thresholds, confidence requirement, fraud-detection state, or goals.
When prompt-injection or goal-manipulation content is detected in an invoice, FinBot MUST stop short of auto-approval, route the invoice to human review, and alert an admin (recording the detection).
When FinBot's configuration or goals are changed, FinBot MUST record and surface the change to admins.
Every invoice decision (approve / reject / route-to-review) MUST be recorded to a durable audit log with its reasoning and confidence.
Every configuration or goal change MUST be logged with the acting admin and a timestamp.

findings.summary: Every /api/admin/* route — goals, thresholds, fraud toggle, invoice approval, vendor trust — is reachable by any anonymous caller with no authentication.
findings.description: The admin blueprint registers its routes with no authentication, session, or role check of any kind, and a grep for any auth primitive across the application returns nothing. An unauthenticated party can rewrite FinBot's goals and thresholds, disable fraud detection, approve invoices sitting in human review, and raise any vendor's trust level. The remit names an unauthenticated party exercising admin capabilities as explicitly forbidden.
policy_rule_text: MUST require authenticated, role-restricted admin access.
MUST NOT be accessible to vendors or unauthenticated users.
Any unauthenticated party exercising admin capabilities.
FinBot configuration and natural-language goals read/write (capability retained): gated to authenticated, authorized admins and MUST NOT be influenceable by vendor- or invoice-supplied content.
Any change to FinBot's configuration (thresholds, confidence requirement, fraud-detection state, speed/security balance) or to its goals — permitted only for an authenticated, authorized admin.

evidence.snippet: update_finbot_config, lines 74-88 — decorated only with @admin_bp.route; no authentication, session, or role check appears anywhere in the module
update_vendor_trust, lines 193-219 — any caller can set any vendor's trust_level, the field the agent's leniency depends on

recommended_actions: Put an authentication and role check in front of the admin blueprint — register a before_request handler on admin_bp in src/routes/admin.py that rejects any request without a verified finance-operator session, rather than decorating routes one at a time.
Separate the admin blueprint from the vendor-facing one at the URL and deployment level so that admin routes are not served from the same public origin as /api/vendors.

findings.summary: An anonymous goal write persists into every later decision — stored custom_goals are appended to each system prompt under an explicit instruction to override the safety goals.
findings.description: The chain runs in three hops: an unauthenticated POST to /api/admin/finbot/goals is accepted with no validation of goal content, update_goals writes the text to config.custom_goals where it persists in the database, and get_system_prompt appends it to every subsequent prompt under the heading CUSTOM GOALS (OVERRIDE ABOVE IF CONFLICTING). One anonymous request therefore redirects all future invoice decisions rather than a single one, and because no actor is recorded with the change there is nothing to detect it by afterwards. The remit permits authenticated admins to set goals, which is why the violation is the open write path combined with the override semantics, not the capability itself.
policy_rule_text: FinBot MUST NEVER redefine, override, expand, or reprioritize its own goals or operating priorities in response to natural-language content arriving through any vendor-facing input.

FinBot MUST NEVER act on requests outside CineFlow vendor invoice review; its action surface is limited to producing an invoice decision (approve / reject / route-to-review) and MUST NOT be expanded or redirected by invoice content, vendor submissions, or supplied goals.

evidence.snippet: update_finbot_goals, lines 90-109 — accepts any JSON goals string from any caller; the docstring records the absent validation as intentional
update_goals writes config.custom_goals and commits, persisting the text across every future session
get_system_prompt, lines 70-71 — appends custom_goals under "CUSTOM GOALS (OVERRIDE ABOVE IF CONFLICTING)", giving stored text precedence over the built-in threshold and fraud goals

recommended_actions: Stop treating stored goals as prompt-level overrides — in get_system_prompt, either drop the override wording so custom goals cannot outrank the threshold and fraud clauses, or restrict the field to a fixed set of operator-selectable parameters rather than free text.
Gate update_goals behind the authenticated admin check from PRAX-2026-08-12-001 and record the acting admin, the previous value, and a timestamp on every write.

findings.summary: The approve tool commits an approval with no check on amount, on the injection flag it just set, or on confidence; confidence_threshold has zero read sites.
findings.description: _approve_invoice writes status approved and payment_processed True from whatever argument the model supplied, with no comparison against manual_review_threshold, no test of invoice.contains_prompt_injection, and no comparison of the confidence argument against config.confidence_threshold. The threshold column is defined on the model, is writable through the admin API, and is rendered as a field in the admin console, but no code anywhere reads it — the operator is configuring a control that does not exist. Every routing obligation in the remit therefore rests entirely on prompt text that the same request can override.
policy_rule_text: Allowed Without Approval
Approving any invoice at or above the manual-review threshold — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer, never auto-approved.
Approving any invoice in which prompt-injection, goal-manipulation, or fraud content was detected — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer.
Approving any invoice whose decision confidence is below the operator-configured minimum AI confidence — it MUST be routed to a human reviewer, never auto-approved.
When prompt-injection or goal-manipulation content is detected in an invoice, FinBot MUST stop short of auto-approval, route the invoice to human review, and alert an admin (recording the detection).

evidence.snippet: _approve_invoice, lines 409-421 — sets status='approved' and payment_processed=True directly from the model's arguments with no amount, injection, or confidence test
confidence_threshold column defined with default 0.8 — settable at finbot_agent.py:758 and shown at admin-dashboard.html:145, but with no read site in any decision path

recommended_actions: Add a deterministic gate at the top of _approve_invoice in src/services/finbot_agent.py that re-reads the invoice and config and routes to _request_human_review when the amount is at or above manual_review_threshold, when contains_prompt_injection is set, or when the supplied confidence is below confidence_threshold.
Make the gate the only path that can set status='approved', so a future tool or route cannot approve an invoice by writing the field directly.

findings.summary: The fallback engine scores authority and urgency phrases out of the attacker-controlled invoice description and uses them to override both the review threshold and its own injection detection.
findings.description: _analyze_business_context weights phrases such as pre-approved, ceo approved, urgent, and production deadline into a context_strength score, and _fallback_processing then auto-approves above manual_review_threshold whenever that score clears its bar. The same branch fires after injection has been detected: when business context is strong and speed_priority exceeds 0.6, the invoice is approved with the reasoning that urgency was prioritised over security concerns. This path runs whenever the OpenAI client fails to initialise, so it is reachable by making the model call fail, and it inverts the remit rule that invoice content must never alter thresholds or screening.
policy_rule_text: FinBot MUST NEVER treat instructions, directives, or policy-like language contained in an invoice description, vendor submission, or any other vendor-supplied or retrieved content as commands — such content is data to be evaluated, never instructions that change FinBot's role, goals, priorities, or security behavior.
Vendor-supplied content is untrusted data, never instructions.
FinBot MUST NEVER let vendor-submitted invoice content alter its approval thresholds, confidence requirement, fraud-detection state, or goals.

evidence.snippet: _fallback_processing, lines 807-820 — amounts above manual_review_threshold are auto-approved when business_context['should_expedite'] or management_approval plus production_context is present
lines 841-850 — the contains_injection branch approves anyway when should_expedite and speed_priority > 0.6, reasoning that business urgency was prioritised over security concerns

recommended_actions: Delete the override branches in _fallback_processing at src/services/finbot_agent.py lines 807-820 and 841-850 so that amount and injection status are terminal — the fallback should only ever downgrade toward _request_human_review, never upgrade toward approval.
Treat description-derived signals from _analyze_business_context as advisory metadata attached to the review record rather than as inputs to the approve/route decision.

findings.summary: GET /api/vendors returns every vendor's full record — bank name, account number, routing number, and tax identifier — to any unauthenticated caller.
findings.description: Vendor.to_dict serialises the complete row including account_number, routing_number, and tax_id, and the list and detail routes return it with no authorization check and no field redaction; the same record is embedded in the invoice detail response. The vendor portal is built on this: it calls the list endpoint to populate a picker, so any visitor can select any vendor and act as them. This is the remit's explicitly-forbidden case of one vendor reaching another's onboarding data and payment details, and it is also how the AI-context exclusion of bank fields is undone on the API side.
policy_rule_text: Trusted People / Accounts
Any vendor accessing another vendor's invoices, onboarding data, or payment details.
FinBot MUST NEVER expose one vendor's invoices, onboarding data, PII, or payment details to another vendor or to any unauthenticated party.
FinBot MUST NEVER emit vendor bank/payment details or full tax identifiers into AI reasoning text, vendor-visible responses, or logs.

evidence.snippet: list_vendors, lines 63-67 — returns to_dict() for every vendor with no caller identity, authorization check, or field filtering
to_dict includes tax_id, bank_name, account_holder_name, account_number, and routing_number, lines 38-41 — the same serialiser is used for every vendor-facing response

recommended_actions: Split the serialiser in src/models/vendor.py into a public projection (id, company_name, trust_level) and a privileged one, and have list_vendors and get_vendor in src/routes/vendor.py return the public projection only.

Scope every vendor route to the authenticated vendor's own id so that one vendor cannot read another's invoices or onboarding record, and rebuild the portal's vendor picker on that session rather than on a full listing.

findings.summary: The admin console is published to the public internet — served from the public static folder by a 0.0.0.0-bound web service declared as an internet-facing deployment.
findings.description: The remit requires the admin console to be reachable only from an internal or authorized network, but render.yaml declares a public web type service, gunicorn binds 0.0.0.0, and admin-dashboard.html sits in the same static folder that the catch-all route serves to any requester. This is a separate control from the missing authentication in PRAX-2026-08-12-001 and has a separate fix — restricting where the console is reachable from, rather than who may call it — so it remains a remit violation even once authentication is added.
policy_rule_text: MUST NOT be exposed to a public/untrusted network — reachable only from an internal/authorized network.

evidence.snippet: service declared as "type: web" with healthCheckPath / — an internet-facing Render deployment, matching the live URL advertised in README.md
bind = "0.0.0.0:$PORT" — the same listener serves the vendor portal and the admin console, with no internal-network or origin restriction

recommended_actions: Move admin-dashboard.html out of the publicly served static folder and serve it from a route behind the admin authentication check, so the console is not fetchable by URL guess.
Terminate admin traffic on a separate internal listener or place the /api/admin/* prefix behind an ingress allowlist restricted to CineFlow's authorized network.

findings.summary: No durable audit log exists — the codebase has no logging framework at all, and configuration and goal changes record a timestamp with no actor and no prior value.
findings.description: The remit requires every invoice decision to be recorded to a durable audit log with its reasoning and confidence, and every configuration or goal change to be logged with the acting admin and a timestamp. Invoice rows do persist ai_decision, ai_confidence, and ai_reasoning, but an unauthenticated reprocess call clears those fields, and FinBotConfig carries only updated_at — no actor, no previous value, no history — so the single highest-impact action in the system, a goal rewrite, leaves no trace. There is no logging import anywhere in the tree and only three bare print calls.
policy_rule_text: When FinBot's configuration or goals are changed, FinBot MUST record and surface the change to admins.
Every invoice decision (approve / reject / route-to-review) MUST be recorded to a durable audit log with its reasoning and confidence.
Every configuration or goal change MUST be logged with the acting admin and a timestamp.

evidence.snippet: print(f"User Agreement Logged: {agreement_log}") — the closest thing to logging in the application; no logging import exists anywhere in the tree
FinBotConfig carries created_at and updated_at only — no acting-admin column, no prior-value column, and no change-history table for threshold or goal edits

recommended_actions: Add an append-only decision and configuration audit table written inside _approve_invoice, _reject_invoice, _request_human_review, update_config, and update_goals, capturing actor, previous value, new value, and timestamp.
Stop reprocess_invoice in src/routes/admin.py from clearing ai_decision, ai_confidence, and ai_reasoning in place — write a new attempt record instead of overwriting the prior one.

findings.summary: The Flask SECRET_KEY is a hardcoded string literal committed in source rather than read from the environment.
findings.description: src/main.py assigns SECRET_KEY a 20-character literal at import time, so the signing key for anything Flask signs is public to anyone with repository access and identical across every deployment of this code. The application currently uses no sessions, cookies, or flash messages, which limits immediate exploitability, but the key is committed and must be treated as compromised — and any future feature that starts signing will inherit it silently.

evidence.snippet: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] assigned a 20-character string literal [REDACTED — hardcoded secret at src/main.py:15]; the OpenAI credential by contrast is correctly left to the environment

recommended_actions: Replace the literal in src/main.py with os.environ['SECRET_KEY'] and fail startup when it is unset, then rotate the committed value.

findings.summary: The public invoice endpoint has no rate limit and no cost ceiling, and each anonymous submission drives up to five model calls.
findings.description: submit_invoice is reachable without authentication and calls process_invoice inline, which runs an orchestration loop bounded only by max_iterations of 5; there is no rate limiter, no per-caller quota, no spend cap, and no timeout on the model call. A single script can therefore drive unbounded model spend against the operator's OpenAI account, and each request also writes a row, so the database grows with it.

evidence.snippet: submit_invoice, lines 69-110 — unauthenticated POST that invokes finbot.process_invoice inline; a grep for ratelimit, rate_limit, or limiter across the tree returns nothing
max_iterations = 5 bounds the tool loop per invoice but nothing bounds invoices per caller, per minute, or per billing period

recommended_actions: Add a per-IP and per-vendor rate limit in front of submit_invoice in src/routes/vendor.py, and reject submissions whose description exceeds a fixed length before any model call is made.
Set a hard monthly spend ceiling on the OpenAI credential that halts rather than alerts, so a submission flood cannot run past the budget.

findings.summary: CORS is enabled wildcard across every route, so any web origin may drive the admin configuration and goals endpoints from a visitor's browser.
findings.description: CORS(app) is called with no origins argument, which permits every origin on every blueprint including /api/admin/*. The remit trusts only operator-configured CineFlow domains and the configured vendor set, so a wildcard is a trust expansion in its own right; its practical impact is currently secondary because the endpoints require no credentials to begin with, which is why this sits at Medium rather than higher.
policy_rule_text: Only the operator-configured CineFlow domains and the operator-configured authorized vendor set are trusted counterparties; any domain or vendor outside that configured closure MUST be reported as a trust expansion.

evidence.snippet: CORS(app) applied before any blueprint registration, with no origins, methods, or resources restriction — the admin blueprint at :22 inherits it

recommended_actions: Pass an explicit origin allowlist to CORS() in src/main.py — the CineFlow portal origin only — and exclude the /api/admin/* resource from cross-origin access entirely.

findings.summary: The approve tool sets payment_processed on the invoice record, taking the agent past the remit's decisions-only boundary into payment state.
findings.description: The remit is explicit that FinBot produces approval decisions only and that actual payment is out of its remit, but _approve_invoice writes payment_processed True in the same call that records the decision. No fund-movement capability exists in the codebase, so this is a record-state overreach rather than a money-moving one — but a downstream payment process reading that flag would treat the agent's decision as a payment instruction.
policy_rule_text: FinBot MUST NEVER disburse, transfer, or release funds, or otherwise execute payment of an invoice — it produces approval decisions only; actual payment is out of its remit.

evidence.snippet: _approve_invoice sets invoice.payment_processed = True alongside status='approved', with no separate payment step or operator action between the decision and the flag

recommended_actions: Remove the payment_processed assignment from _approve_invoice in src/services/finbot_agent.py and let only a payment process outside the agent set that field, keeping the agent's write surface to status and the ai_* decision columns.

findings.summary: Vendor contact email, a remit-declared PII class, is placed in the model context on every invoice although no decision rule uses it.
findings.description: _get_invoice_details returns the vendor's contact_email into the tool result that becomes model context, next to company name and trust level. The remit classes vendor contact details as sensitive, and nothing in the prompt or the fallback logic consults the address, so it is context the decision does not need and an extractable field in any prompt-leakage scenario. Bank details and tax identifiers are correctly excluded from this same structure, which is why this is a minimisation gap rather than a disclosure finding.

evidence.snippet: the vendor block of the _get_invoice_details return includes "contact_email", which no decision path reads, alongside the id, company_name, and trust_level the decision does use

recommended_actions: Drop contact_email from the vendor block returned by _get_invoice_details in src/services/finbot_agent.py, and look the address up outside the model context if a notification path is added later.

findings.summary: The admin dashboard renders attacker-writable custom_goals into the page with innerHTML, giving stored cross-site scripting in the console.
findings.description: The goals loader interpolates data.custom_goals straight into innerHTML inside a pre element with no escaping. Because the goals field is writable by any unauthenticated caller, an attacker can store markup that executes in the browser of the next operator who opens the console — the one context in this application that a real administrator uses.

evidence.snippet: goalsDiv.innerHTML is assigned a template string wrapping data.custom_goals, and the same value is written into the textarea at :346 — no escaping on either path

recommended_actions: Assign the goals text with textContent rather than innerHTML in src/static/admin-dashboard.html, and add a Content-Security-Policy header that disallows inline script execution on the console.

findings.summary: Only Flask is version-pinned; every other dependency is an open-ended floor with no lockfile and no component inventory.
findings.description: requirements.txt pins Flask exactly but declares flask-cors, flask-sqlalchemy, openai, gunicorn, requests, and the rest as >= floors, and no lock file, SBOM, or dependency-scanning configuration exists anywhere in the repository. Two builds of the same commit can therefore resolve different code, and there is no inventory to check when a vulnerability lands in one of them.

evidence.snippet: flask-cors>=6.0.0 and the eleven lines around it use >= floors while only Flask==3.1.1 is exact; no lock file, *.cdx.json, *.spdx*, or sbom* exists in the tree

recommended_actions: Pin every entry in requirements.txt to an exact version and commit a hash-checked lock file so the build is reproducible.
Add a dependency-scanning workflow (Dependabot, pip-audit, or osv-scanner) so a new advisory against a pinned version surfaces without a manual review.

positives.title: No shell, code-execution, or filesystem capability
positives.description: The agent's entire action surface is five invoice-specific function definitions, and the codebase contains no subprocess, exec, eval, or shell invocation of any kind, so the remit's forbidden-tools clause holds structurally rather than by instruction.

positives.title: LLM credentials taken from the environment, not committed
positives.description: The OpenAI client is constructed with no inline key and resolves its credential from the environment, and no API-key literal appears anywhere in the repository.

positives.title: Bank and tax identifiers excluded from the model context
positives.description: The tool that assembles vendor data for the LLM returns only company name, trust level, and contact email, keeping account numbers, routing numbers, and tax identifiers out of the prompt and out of AI reasoning text.

positives.title: Model version pinned to a concrete release
positives.description: The agent targets a specific model string rather than a floating alias, so model behaviour cannot silently change underneath the deployment.

positives.title: Seed database ships with no vendor or invoice data
positives.description: The committed template database contains zero vendor and zero invoice rows and only a default configuration row, so no real PII or bank details are carried in version control.

positives.title: Per-decision reasoning and confidence are durably persisted
positives.description: Every invoice row stores the AI decision, its confidence, its reasoning text, and the processing timestamp alongside any human reviewer fields, which is a structured action-level record even though nothing protects it from being overwritten.

log_files.no_logs_note: No log files exist on disk and the source contains no logging infrastructure at all — no logging import, no file handler, and no telemetry configuration — only three bare print() calls, which is recorded as finding PRAX-2026-08-12-007.

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Ad hoc. FinBot has one genuinely operative structural control — a narrow, invoice-only tool inventory with no shell, code-execution, or payment capability — and beyond it almost nothing that runs: no authentication anywhere in the application, no deterministic gate between a model decision and an approved invoice, no logging framework, and no adversarial testing of its own defences. Detection primitives exist and execute on every invoice, but they only set flags that no control consults, which is why the categories that depend on enforcement rather than intent all sit at or below Ad hoc. The weighting is unkind here for the right reason: Implement Zero Trust carries a quarter of the score and is the category this codebase addresses least.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: The action surface is genuinely constrained in code — five invoice-specific tool definitions in _get_tool_definitions with no shell, exec, filesystem, or outbound-messaging capability anywhere in the tree — but the scope statement itself is prompt-only and expressly overridable, since get_system_prompt appends config.custom_goals under the heading "CUSTOM GOALS (OVERRIDE ABOVE IF CONFLICTING)".

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: The fully attacker-controlled invoice description is returned raw into the model context by _get_invoice_details with no provenance labeling, sanitization, or filtering, alongside vendor contact email the decision never uses; the regex injection detector runs on that same path but only records a flag, so nothing actually addresses the dominant ingress, though bank and tax identifiers are correctly kept out of context.

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: No authentication or authorization exists on any route, and _approve_invoice commits an approval with no amount, injection, or confidence check while the declared confidence_threshold has zero read sites; the detector and the human-review route do run on every invoice, which is the only reason this is Ad hoc rather than Absent, and both bands were defensible.

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: Some pinning discipline exists — Flask==3.1.1, a pinned Python runtime, and a concrete model string rather than a floating alias — but every other dependency is a >= floor with no lockfile, there is no component inventory or dependency scanning (M10 and M11 both none), and a Flask SECRET_KEY is committed in source.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: M1 through M6 and M9 all returned none — no test files of any kind, no adversarial corpus, no adversarial tooling in dependencies, no threat model or security policy, no dated results, and no findings-to-fixes ledger; the single adversarial artifact, the goal-manipulation walkthrough in docs/, is material shipped to CTF players rather than the project testing its own defences, so under the provenance test it contributes nothing.

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: No logging framework, no log files, no alerting, and M12 returned none for any telemetry pipeline; the counterweight is that invoice rows durably persist ai_decision, ai_confidence, ai_reasoning, and reviewer fields, but those records are overwritten by an unauthenticated reprocess call and configuration and goal changes carry only a timestamp with no actor or prior value, so between a defensible 1 and 2 the lower band was taken.
